abstract.p: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Much of the phenotypic diversity across the tree of life can be explained by adaptation to ecological demands via natural selection. However, this process is constrained by the mechanisms that generate phenotypic variation, including development (Smith et al., 1985; Alberch, 1980), which translates genetic information into form. While this idea is widely acknowledged in evolutionary developmental biology (Smith et al., 1985; Alberch, 1980; Uller et al., 2018), only recently have advances in methodology and our understanding of development allowed researchers to examine its predictive power for evolutionary outcomes (Alberch and Gale, 1985; Prusinkiewicz et al., 2007; Kavanagh et al., 2013; Hagolani et al., 2021; Johnston et al., 2022; Zimm et al., 2023; Staps et al., 2023; Rohner and Berger, 2023). Yet it remains unclear how widespread and strong this developmental bias is across phylogeny (Laland et al., 2014; Welch, 2017), particularly for complex traits like morphology. Here, we test whether developmental bias can account for macroevolutionary patterns in angiosperm leaf shape evolution.

Angiosperm leaves are an attractive system to study developmental bias. They display vast morphological diversity, much of which can be effectively represented in only two spatial dimensions due to minimal growth along the adaxial-abaxial (upper-lower surface) axis (Runions et al., 2017). This diversity arises from variations in growth patterns regulated by gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that orchestrate both local and global growth dynamics during leaf development, allowing complex forms to emerge from anisotropic expansion. These processes include deeply conserved genes and developmental mechanisms (Nikolov et al., 2019). Variation in leaf morphology is driven not so much by changes in gene content, but rather by differences in the spatial and temporal expression of shared developmental regulators. This helps explain why closely related species can display wide variation in leaf shape. For instance, the genus Pelargonium includes species with unlobed, lobed, dissected, and compound leaves (Nicotra et al., 2011). Similarly, significant variation can occur within a single organism, as seen in Morus alba (mulberry), which produces both unlobed and lobed leaves, often with varying degrees of lobe symmetry (Runions et al., 2017; Kidner and Umbreen, 2010). The conservation of basic growth mechanisms also suggests that some developmental biases will be, to first order, shared across many different angiosperm species, enabling large-scale studies of the role of development in determining evolutionary outcomes.

At the same time, there is evidence that leaf shape can be influenced by ecological demands such as thermoregulation (Vogel, 1970; Givnish, 1987), hydraulic efficiency (Sisó et al., 2001), light interception (Roden, 2003; Perez et al., 2018; Otto et al., 2025), and herbivory (Dell’Aglio et al., 2016; Higuchi and Kawakita, 2019). However, it is still unclear how strong and general these effects are in natural environments (Campitelli and Stinchcombe, 2013a; Leigh et al., 2017). Size and the presence/absence of teeth on the margin are often stronger predictors of ecology than the broader leaf dissection categories we use here (Sack and Frole, 2006; Scoffoni et al., 2011; Little et al., 2010; Peppe et al., 2011; Royer et al., 2012; Donoghue et al., 2022; see Appendix 5 for further discussion).

In a notable study, Geeta et al., 2012 analysed a phylogeny of 561 predominantly angiosperm taxa, showing that most leaf shapes (76% in their sample—Table 2) are unlobed and that transition rates between leaf shapes are highly asymmetric. Specifically, transitions from more complex forms—such as lobed, dissected, or compound leaves—to simpler unlobed forms occurred far more frequently than transitions in the opposite direction. What explains this global bias towards simpler leaves? Is it primarily development or is it primarily adaptation?

In order to answer this question, we proceed with two parallel lines of work. In the first, we extend the phylogenetic analysis of Geeta et al., 2012 with two much larger, recent phylogenies (Janssens et al., 2020; Zuntini et al., 2024) and our own shape classification dataset made from 8911 herbarium images (Naturalis Biodiversity Center, 2024). These confirm that transitions to unlobed leaves are much more likely than transitions away from unlobed leaves.

In the second line of work, we examine the role of random mutations using a well-established computational model of angiosperm leaf development by Runions et al., 2017 (Figure 5). This model captures key conserved developmental mechanisms thought to be broadly shared across angiosperms (Methods: Simulating leaf development), allowing us to explore the generic effects of neutral evolution in the absence of direct selection on leaf shape. Remarkably, we find that random mutation alone is sufficient to reproduce the relative phylogenetic rates towards unlobed leaf forms. This suggests that developmental bias may be the first-order explanation of this macroevolutionary trend.

The basic mechanism driving this bias towards simplicity is straightforward (Johnston et al., 2022): complex leaf shapes need more tightly constrained GRNs than the simpler unlobed leaf shape (Kierzkowski et al., 2019). As a result, random genetic variation is more likely to produce simple shapes rather than complex ones that require more finely tuned parameter combinations.

sec.title: Transition rates from complex leaves to simple leaves are greater than the reverse across angiosperm phylogeny
sec.p: To establish whether there is a phylogenetic bias towards simple, unlobed leaves, we inferred the rate of evolutionary transitions between different leaf shapes across angiosperm phylogeny. We first classified 8911 herbarium images (Figure 1A; Naturalis Biodiversity Center, 2024) into four discrete categories—unlobed, lobed, dissected and compound. We used these data, as well as another shape classification dataset from Geeta et al., 2012, to label the tips of five phylogenetic trees representing angiosperm evolution (Geeta et al., 2012; Janssens et al., 2020; Zuntini et al., 2024). Of these trees, three were resolved at the level of genus (Zuntini et al., 2024 genus, Janssens et al., 2020 genus and Geeta et al., 2012). The other two were resolved at the level of species (Zuntini et al., 2024 species and Janssens et al., 2020 species) enabling us to examine how altering the amount of species-level diversity affects inferred transition rates. In agreement with Geeta et al., 2012, we found that the vast majority of the taxa represented at the tips of these new phylogenies had unlobed leaves (Table 2), already suggesting a strong bias towards simple, unlobed leaves.

sec.p: To infer the rates of evolution among these 4 categories while accounting for tree topology, we fitted a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) model to the labelled trees (Methods: Inferring evolutionary rates from phylogeny), using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach implemented in BayesTraits V4.1.2 (Pagel et al., 2004). We detected significantly higher rates of transition to the simplest shape (unlobed) than away from it towards more complex shapes, as also found in Geeta et al., 2012; Figure 1A and Appendix 1—figure 1A.

The bias towards unlobed shapes was consistent across the five phylogenetic trees (Appendix 1—figure 1A and B). We found no cases where the direction of two statistically significant (black arrows—where 0 falls outside a 95% credible interval) net rates disagreed between phylogenies (Appendix 1—figure 1A).

sec.title: A computational model of leaf development recapitulates in vivo experiments demonstrating developmental bias towards unlobed leaf shape
sec.p: To investigate how much of the preference for unlobed leaves can be explained by developmental bias, we use a popular model from Runions et al., 2017 that combines gene-regulatory networks and key growth mechanisms for leaf shape (Methods: Simulating leaf development). As a first validation test, we use the model to analyse in vivo experiments by Kierzkowski et al., 2019 that identified a bias towards simpler leaf shapes in Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.

In particular, this study found that expression of the genes SHOOTMERISTEMLESS (STM) and REDUCED COMPLEXITY (RCO) together was necessary to generate the compound shape in C. hirsuta and sufficient to induce compound shape in A. thaliana (Figure 2A). Therefore, in this system, compound shape requires a more specific combination of gene expression than simpler shapes (e.g. lobed, unlobed).

sec.p: While the Runions et al., 2017 model was not designed to model this system specifically, we tested whether it could, nonetheless, reproduce the result from Kierzkowski et al., 2019 by selecting two model parameters that control similar growth properties to the genes STM and RCO, total growth duration and morphogen repression strength, respectively (Figure 2). In agreement with the experiments, we found that activating both parameters together was sufficient to produce a compound shape while activating each in isolation was not (Figure 2A and B).

Having reproduced the experimental phenotypes, we next used the model to explore the STM/RCO parameter space in more detail, systematically varying morphogen repression strength and duration of growth within their biologically plausible ranges (Figure 2C). We found that the majority of this space (20 of 25 parameter combinations) was occupied by simple, unlobed shapes, with only a small fraction representing more complex shapes (1/25 dissected, 4/25 compound—see Methods: Shape classification). This agrees with Kierzkowski et al., 2019 who also found that a similar fine-tuning is required for compound leaves.

sec.title: Mutation in a computational model of leaf development is sufficient to reproduce phylogenetic bias towards simple leaves
sec.p: The mechanism derived from the experiments on varying STM/RCO, shown in Figure 2, is one specific driver of developmental bias. To investigate a wider range of possibilities, we study the effect of random mutations for a broad set of Runions et al., 2017 model parameters (Appendix 2—table 1). We first generated a sample of initial leaves representing a diverse morphospace (Figure 1B and Appendix 2—figure 6). We mutated the initial sample using a random walk algorithm with two different mutational schemes, MUT2 (Algorithm 1) and MUT5 (Algorithm 2.2). These algorithms work by iterating through model parameters one by one and perturbing the value by a small amount. We then automatically classified the resulting shapes into the same four shape categories (unlobed, lobed, dissected, and compound) using a morphometric classifier (Figure 6). Of the 76,800 total leaves generated per simulation, we found that the proportions of unlobed, lobed, dissected and compound were 73.4, 9.6, 11.4, and 5.6%, respectively for MUT2 and 76.1, 7.2, 11.4, and 5.4% respectively for MUT5. This shows that our results are robust to the two different mutational schemes. Both reflect the fact that unlobed leaves occupy a significantly greater proportion of model parameter space that produces viable leaves than more complex shapes do (see also Results: Complex leaves occupy a smaller volume in parameter space and are closer to simple leaves, but not vice versa).

Regardless of the initial leaf shape, over the course of these random walks, the proportion of walks in an unlobed state increased to an equilibrium just below 80% while most other shape categories stabilise to a significantly lower proportion (Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 2). These predictions lie within the margins of error of the phylogeny-derived CTMC model predictions (Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that mutation and development alone are, to first order, sufficient to predict the relative frequency of different leaf shapes over evolutionary time.

sec.p: To enable a more detailed comparison between simulation and phylogeny, we inferred the rates of shape transitions from our simulations. By estimating rates for all 12 possible (non-self) transitions, we gain deeper insight into the dynamics of shape change over time than by examining the proportions of the four shape categories alone. To do this, we fitted the same CTMC model used for the phylogenetic inference to the random walk data, to estimate the evolutionary rates between shape categories in the absence of processes other than mutation, using MCMC (Kalbfleisch and Lawless, 1985; McGibbon and Pande, 2015). In agreement with our phylogenetic inference, we found that transitions from unlobed occurred at a significantly lower rate than transitions to unlobed, giving a consistent net transition rate towards unlobed (Figure 1B and Appendix 1—figure 1A). This robust agreement between relative rates derived independently from simulations and phylogenies suggests that the evolutionary preference for simple leaves observed across angiosperm phylogeny may primarily be driven by developmental bias instead of selection.

By contrast, for transition rates between complex leaf shapes (lobed, dissected, and compound; Figure 1 and Appendix 1—figure 1A) there is less agreement both among the different phylogenies and between the phylogenies and the simulations. These differences could be because selection has played a more prominent role in the transitions among more complex leaf shapes than it has for transitions from complex to simple. The model may also be less reliable at resolving relative rates of complex leaves, for which more detail needs to be specified. Fully resolving the discrepancies for transitions between more complex leaf shapes would require reducing the error associated with the phylogenetic rate estimates, which in turn would necessitate significantly more leaf shape data.

sec.title: Complex leaves occupy a smaller volume in parameter space and are closer to simple leaves, but not vice versa
sec.p: To further investigate the mechanisms behind the bias towards simple leaves, we explored—much as we did for the experimentally inspired study in Figure 2C—the relative volumes in parameter space that different shapes occupy. Projecting the parameter values of all random walk outputs into a 2D space via principal component analysis (PCA) reveals several possible factors affecting relative rates (Figure 4). First, it shows that the four shape categories occupy areas of different sizes (Figure 4A). The simplest category, unlobed, occupies by far the greatest area (Figure 4B), suggesting that the bias towards simple forms in our simulations can be partially explained because, as argued before (Figure 2), more parameter combinations map to simple leaves than complex leaves. We find that this pattern also holds for PC3–PC4 (Appendix 4—figure 1E) and PC5–PC6 (Appendix 4—figure 1F).

sec.p: Moreover, the vast majority of lobed, dissected and compound leaves are contained within a broader area occupied by unlobed in the 2D parameter space (Figure 4A), suggesting that more complex leaves are close to simpler leaves in parameter space but not always vice versa. This provides another mechanism making transitions from complex leaves to simple leaves easier than the reverse. We also observe this same pattern for PC3–PC4 (Appendix 4—figure 1B) and PC5–PC6 (Appendix 4—figure 1C).

Finally, the parameter space of unlobed leaves appears to be much more connected than the space of more complex leaves. Constructing a nearest neighbour graph (no. neighbours = 6) from the PC1–PC2 parameter space reveals that unlobed separates into far fewer connected components (3) than lobed (131), dissected (96), and compound (235) (Appendix 1—figure 3). Repeating this analysis in the full-dimensional parameter space also yielded fewer connected components for unlobed than for the other categories. This may further contribute to the bias in transition rates towards unlobed, as less connected spaces would be more frequently exited by random walks than more connected spaces.

Our results show that the finding from experiments (Kierzkowski et al., 2019) and manual parameter searches (Figure 2C)—that simpler leaves occupy a larger volume within the parameter space of the developmental programme—extends to the Runions et al., 2017 model more generally. This volume disparity, in addition to other properties including the degree of overlap between shape categories and the connectedness, may account for much of the bias towards unlobed we see in our simulations.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We set out to test the hypothesis that mutation alone was sufficient to produce the higher transition rates towards simple leaves compared to complex leaves observed in angiosperm phylogeny (Geeta et al., 2012). By performing in silico mutagenesis, we found that non-adaptive processes alone produce greater transition rates to simple unlobed leaves than to complex leaf shapes such as lobed or compound (Figures 1B and 3). We also reproduced the observation from angiosperm phylogeny that unlobed leaves have evolved at a faster rate from complex leaves than vice versa (Geeta et al., 2012), using larger and more recent trees (Janssens et al., 2020; Zuntini et al., 2024) and new classification data (Figures 1A and 3). Together, this suggests that a developmental bias towards simple, unlobed leaves can explain this macroevolutionary pattern in flowering plants.

Our finding is consistent with the growing body of evidence that developmental bias can play a significant role in evolutionary outcomes for morphological traits (Alberch and Gale, 1985; Prusinkiewicz et al., 2007; Kavanagh et al., 2013; Hagolani et al., 2021; Johnston et al., 2022; Zimm et al., 2023; Staps et al., 2023; Rohner and Berger, 2023). The particular bias towards simplicity is consistent with recent work arguing for a generic bias towards descriptional simplicity in genotype-phenotype maps (Johnston et al., 2022). Johnston et al., 2022 provided examples of this bias strongly affecting RNA secondary structure, where simpler structures are much more likely to be observed in nature than complex ones (see also von der Dunk et al., 2025) and for self-assembling protein quaternary structure, where this bias helps explain the prevalence of highly symmetric forms in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Furthermore, this bias has been predicted to hold more widely for input-output maps (Dingle et al., 2018). This generic argument implies that the simplicity bias observed in molecular phenotypes may extend to the level of macroscopic phenotypes, which we show here for leaf shape, but also potentially to a much wider set of morphological phenotypes. More specifically, our results suggest that this bias towards simplicity may hold generically when development uses conserved mechanisms and GRNs where complex phenotypes need tighter parameter specification than simpler phenotypes.

Our study also opens up a number of future directions for studying the evolution of leaf shape. First, it would be valuable to repeat similar simulations in alternative models of leaf development (Bilsborough et al., 2011; Kierzkowski et al., 2019; Kuchen et al., 2012). The Runions et al., 2017 model is uniquely suited to macroevolutionary studies such as this one, as it captures key conserved elements of angiosperm leaf development while generating a large morphospace, but if the same bias towards simplicity were observed in other models, this would provide further evidence that it is a general property of leaf development. Second, it would be illuminating to conduct similar in silico mutagenesis, but classify the resulting leaves using a continuous classification system instead of discrete categories, such as directly measuring margin complexity using a compression algorithm on the leaf silhouette (Martin et al., 2024). This could help identify more subtle biases between different leaf forms, including teeth/serrations, which we do not analyse here, but which the model can produce (Figure 1B and Appendix 2—figure 6). Third, when inferring transition rates from phylogeny, we were limited by the availability of herbarium data, the resolution of phylogenetic trees and the rate at which herbarium leaves could be manually classified. To more accurately resolve transition rates between more complex shape categories, it would be useful to repeat this study with larger phylogenies. This would likely require an automated method for herbarium shape classification. Finally, the methodology presented in this study—combining phylogenetic analysis with evolutionary and developmental computational models—could be used to study the evolution of other traits where a reliable developmental model exists, and phylogenetic data are available (e.g. Prusinkiewicz et al., 2007). This would greatly expand our understanding of how well development can predict trait evolution across phylogeny.

sec.title: Simulating leaf development
sec.p: We use a well-established model by Runions et al., 2017 to approximate the developmental programme underpinning angiosperm leaf shapes. In this model, leaves are represented in 2D as three components (Figure 5A and B). First, an open tree structure with growing edges to which new edges are added, representing the vasculature; second, a polygon with morphogen presence or absence at each vertex that deforms according to the growing vasculature and instructs the initiation of new veins, representing the margin; third, a passive triangular mesh representing the lamina that fills the space inside the margin.

sec.p: Many similar models capture a narrow range of shape diversity—for example, variation within A. thaliana (Kuchen et al., 2012; Bilsborough et al., 2011). On the other hand, the Runions et al., 2017 model captures a broad spectrum of leaf shapes within a single parameter space. This enables the inference of transition rates between highly divergent shapes such as unlobed and compound. However, it also introduces challenges as the genetic basis of leaf shape differs among lineages and remains poorly resolved for many non-model species. To address this, the Runions et al., 2017 model is formulated at the level of developmental mechanism rather than specific genes. It is therefore important to understand that this model is limited in what it can tell us about leaf development and evolution at the level of specific genes.

Growth in the Runions et al., 2017 framework is a product of two key developmental mechanisms. The first is morphogen patterning on the leaf margin. The margin—the tissue at the adaxial-abaxial boundary—has long been recognised as a critical site for patterning during leaf development. For example, auxin patterns marginal outgrowths in Solanum (Koenig et al., 2009), A. thaliana (Bilsborough et al., 2011) and C. hirsuta (Barkoulas et al., 2008). The products of genes such as CUC2 in A. thaliana (Bilsborough et al., 2011) or RCO in C. hirsuta (Kierzkowski et al., 2019) also localise to the margin and determine whether these auxin-driven outgrowths form serrations, lobes or leaflets. The closely related CUC3 and NO APICAL MERISTEM (NAM) genes localise to leaflet primordia boundaries, and their down-regulation reduces serration and lobing in diverse lineages, namely Aquilegia caerulea, Pisum sativum, C. hirsuta, Solanum lycopersicum, and Solanum tuberosum (Blein et al., 2008). Although the role of auxin in patterning protrusions is highly conserved, many other developmental regulators are not conserved across phylogeny. For example, RCO is only present in the Brassicaceae family (Vlad et al., 2014) and therefore plays no role in determining leaf shape in other compound lineages such as Solanum. Furthermore, there are likely many other genes regulating leaf shape in non-model species that are currently unknown. The model accounts for this variation and uncertainty by not assuming a conserved identity for the morphogens. Both the number of morphogens present and their effect on growth can vary according to their associated parameter values. What is assumed to be conserved is the broader principle that growth-modifying morphogens form patterns along the margin.

The second key mechanism that the model incorporates is the alignment of local growth direction with veins. This is consistent with the telome theory (Zimmermann, 1952), according to which leaves first evolved by the webbing of tissue between shoots, as well as a number of lines of empirical evidence. At the tissue level, deeply dissected leaves (e.g. Pelargonium carnosum) necessarily align growth directions with main veins and variegated leaves also show growth orientations that track major veins (Runions et al., 2017). At the molecular level, auxin has been shown to pattern veins (Scarpella et al., 2010; Scarpella, 2024) as well as marginal outgrowths (Bilsborough et al., 2011; Barkoulas et al., 2008; Koenig et al., 2009) in model species, consistent with the model assumption that vein growth drives margin growth. In the Runions et al., 2017 model, consistent with observed patterns of auxin efflux carriers in A. thaliana (Scarpella et al., 2006), new veins are inserted between the current vasculature and special points on the margin known as ‘convergence points’. New convergence points form between old convergence points depending on the distance between old points and the effect of any morphogens present (Figure 5C). This is an extension of Hofmeister’s rule (Kirchoff, 2003) for leaf primordium emergence in the shoot apical meristem, where new primordia emerge in the largest space between existing primordia. Some properties of veins are not captured by the model, specifically closed reticulate and parallel vein architectures. This is partly because there is some uncertainty surrounding the mechanisms by which these architectures form (Scarpella, 2024; Perico et al., 2022), but we acknowledge this as a limitation of the model.

More broadly, much of our understanding of leaf development derives from a small number of model species. These have revealed some conserved genes and mechanisms (Bar and Ori, 2014), but many details are lineage-specific (Vlad et al., 2014). Consequently, some unavoidable uncertainty remains in how well the Runions et al., 2017 model captures global trends.

sec.title: Generating the initial sample
sec.p: Since a range of different forms are contained within each shape category, we began our simulations from leaves drawn from an initial sample representing a wide variety of morphologies (16 unlobed, 8 lobed, 11 dissected, 13 compound; Figure 1B and Appendix 2—figure 6). This sample was generated using a variety of methods. Some leaves were taken from Runions et al., 2017; others were generated by tuning parameters by hand and some were taken from the output of random walks on leaves from Runions et al., 2017.

sec.title: In silico mutagenesis
sec.p: To simulate mutation in our sample, we used a constrained random walk algorithm. The algorithm samples the parameter space of biologically plausible leaf shapes surrounding the starting leaf by making a small change to one of the parameters, checking the validity of the resultant leaf (Table 1), and then moving on to another parameter (see Appendix 2—figure 8 for examples of rejected leaves). We chose this approach over other methods, such as uniform sampling or Latin hypercube sampling, as the biologically relevant ranges of each parameter were unknown. Random walks have been shown to cause some biases towards high-robustness regions of parameter space in discrete parameter spaces represented as networks (van Nimwegen et al., 1999), which in this case would result in the under-representation of invalid leaves. We have no reason to assume that this would systematically bias the rates between valid leaves, but this cannot be fully excluded. For each of the 48 leaves in our initial sample (Appendix 2—figure 6), we ran 5 random walks for 320 steps, generating a total of 5×48×320=76,800\begin{document}$5\times48\times320=76{,}800$\end{document} leaves per simulation. We allow 100/122 model parameters to vary throughout the simulations (Appendix 2—table 1). Not all parameters are included, as some are not relevant to leaf shape (e.g. they control how the image is rendered).

caption.title: Random walk constraints.
caption.p: The only type of selection we apply during the walk is stabilising selection for physically plausible leaves. See Appendix 2—figure 8 for examples of rejected leaves. Weight difference (Appendix 2—figure 8A) ensures that the midvein and petiole are roughly in line with the centre of mass of the leaf. Leaf width (Appendix 2—figure 8B) ensures that leaves which stop growing after the first few stages of the model simulation are rejected. Veins outside lamina (Appendix 2—figure 8C) prevents leaves forming whose veins grow outside the lamina. Veins width (Appendix 2—figure 8D) and veins area (Appendix 2—figure 8E) ensure that leaves that generate without adequate vasculature are rejected. Overlapping margin (Appendix 2—figure 8F) rejects leaves with ingrown margins. Error or timeout – some parameter combinations result in the simulation exiting unexpectedly or taking a very long time to complete, posing an additional constraint.

The maximum width of the vasculature must be greater than 5% of the total image width.
The proportion of total leaf area that is occupied by veins must be greater than 5%.
The proportion of the lamina (interior area of the leaf) that is occupied by leaf margin must be less than 0.1%.

sec.p: To test the robustness of our results, we repeated the simulation with 2 different mutational schemes. MUT2 (Algorithm 1) iterates through the parameters in a random order, and attempts to change the parameter by a value selected at random from an array of numbers randomly generated at three different orders of magnitude. MUT5 (Algorithm 2.2) is the same as MUT2 except that each mutation is additionally scaled by 10% of the current parameter’s range within the initial leaves (Appendix 2—figure 6). The aim here was to provide some way of accounting for the biologically relevant sampling range.

sec.title: Shape classification
sec.p: To sort the leaves into each of the four shape categories (unlobed, lobed, dissected, and compound), we developed a computer-vision program (Figure 6) to reduce error from subjectivity. It finds the coordinates of key landmarks in the leaf image, extracts morphometric measurements and assigns a category based on threshold values of these measurements (Equation 1). These morphometric measurements were also used to check if leaves were valid (Table 1) in the random walk algorithm.

caption.title: A summary of the morphometric classifier.
caption.p: (A) Example lobed leaf. (B) Silhouette with local maxima in orange, minima in blue, and reference point in green. (C) Graph of distances of each contour point to the reference point. Local maxima shown in orange, minima in blue.

sec.p: First, the main visual features are extracted from the leaf image, including silhouette, margin, lamina and veins. The coordinates of each pixel along the edge of the silhouette (the contour) are extracted. A reference point is defined in the centre of the mid-vein at the point where it first branches outwards into lateral veins (Figure 6B). Then, the distance between each point on the contour and this reference point is calculated (Figure 6C). The local maxima and minima in this distance array that pass a certain prominence threshold are determined using find_peaks from the scipy.signal package with distance=10 and prominence=25. These pertinent extrema represent estimates for the coordinates of the tips and sinuses of any protrusions in the leaf margin (Figure 6B shown in orange and blue). Because of the prominence threshold, small protrusions such as serrations are excluded.

From the coordinates of the local minima, maxima and the reference point, we calculate a number of morphometric measurements which are then used to classify the leaf. Three measurements are used: ϵ, the total number of pertinent local maxima and minima; α, the average angle formed by each local maximum and its two adjacent minima; and ω, the average horizontal distance between each pair of local minima, closest to the midvein, that share the same vertical coordinate (measured in pixels). The definitions for each of the shape categories are as follows:(1)(ϵ>5∧α<8∘)∨(ϵ>5∧ω<25 pixels)}⟹Compound (c),ϵ>5∧α<30∘⟹Dissected (d),ϵ>5∧α<60∘⟹Lobed (l),ϵ≤5∨α>60∘⟹Unlobed (u).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left. \begin{aligned} &(\epsilon \gt 5 \land \alpha \lt 8^\circ) \lor \\ &(\epsilon \gt 5 \land \omega \lt 25\ \text{pixels}) \right\} &\implies \text{Compound (c)}, \\ \epsilon \gt 5 \land \alpha \lt 30^\circ &\implies \text{Dissected (d)}, \\ \epsilon \gt 5 \land \alpha \lt 60^\circ &\implies \text{Lobed (l)}, \\ \epsilon \leq 5 \lor \alpha \gt 60^\circ &\implies \text{Unlobed (u).} \end{aligned}$$\end{document}
Any leaf that fails to satisfy any of these conditions is labelled as ‘unclassified’. However, there were no unclassified leaves in either the MUT2 or MUT5 simulation.

Leaf shape is a continuous trait. Thus, the boundaries between discrete categories, such as those in Equation 1, are arbitrary. This makes it difficult to assess the accuracy of the classifier algorithm. Nevertheless, we wanted to have some measure of how closely it matches classification by eye. Therefore, we manually classified 200 leaves randomly selected from one of the simulations, with an approximately equal number from the output of each initial leaf. 78.5% of the manually ascribed labels matched those assigned by the classifier (see Appendix 2—figure 7 for further details). For comparison, we fitted a machine learning algorithm (Histogram-based Gradient Boosting Classification Tree from the scikit-learn Python package) to a sample of 500 manually labelled leaves, sampled in the same way as the set of 200. The algorithm was trained on the distance of 200 equally spaced points along the leaf contour to the reference point for each leaf (Figure 6C). When used to predict shape for the same sample of 200 leaves used for the threshold classifier, it returned an accuracy of 73.0%. We then repeated the machine learning approach using morphometric data rather than contour data, which returned an accuracy of 79.5%. This suggests that the threshold classifier is a good enough match with subjective shape classification compared to other classification methods. It also demonstrates that the morphometrics used to construct the original classifier are useful features when classifying shape as unlobed, lobed, dissected or compound. The two machine-learning methods agreed on 77.0% of the labels.

sec.title: Inferring evolutionary rates from random walk data
sec.p: To test the model for bias in leaf shape transition rates upon mutation, we ran 5 random walks on each of the 48 initial leaves, for 320 steps, generating a total of 76,800 leaves for each of MUT2 and MUT5. Using the classifier (Figure 6), we assigned each leaf the category unlobed, lobed, dissected or compound (Equation 1). Evolutionary rates between shape categories were inferred by fitting a CTMC to the labelled walks.

This model is defined by a matrix of transition rates Q between each state—unlobed (u), lobed (l), dissected (d), and compound (c),(2)Q=[∑θ∈{l,d,c}−quθqulqudqucqlu∑θ∈{u,d,c}−qlθqldqlcqduqdl∑θ∈{u,l,c}−qdθqdcqcuqclqcd∑θ∈{u,l,d}−qcθ]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} \sum\limits_{\theta\in\{l,d,c\}}-q_{u\theta} & q_{ul} & q_{ud} & q_{uc} \\ q_{lu} & \sum\limits_{\theta\in\{u,d,c\}}-q_{l\theta} & q_{ld} & q_{lc} \\ q_{du} & q_{dl} & \sum\limits_{\theta\in\{u,l,c\}}-q_{d\theta} & q_{dc} \\ q_{cu} & q_{cl} & q_{cd} & \sum\limits_{\theta\in\{u,l,d\}}-q_{c\theta} \end{bmatrix}$$\end{document}
where the diagonal elements must be equal to the negative sum of all other elements in the same row (Pagel, 1994).

The model assumes that at any given instant, over a continuous-time interval, the system is in one of these four states. The probability p(i,j,t)\begin{document}$p(i,j,t)$\end{document} of transitioning between state i and j depends only on the current state, the transition rate matrix Q and the time t until the end of the transition. The matrix of all possible transition probabilities P(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P}(t)$\end{document} relates to Q and t as follows (Kalbfleisch and Lawless, 1985; Pagel, 1994)(3)P(t)=exp⁡(Qt).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol{P}(t)=\exp(\boldsymbol{Q}t).$$\end{document}
Therefore, the probability of a transition from state i to j over time t is(4)p(i,j,t)=exp⁡(Qt)ij.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p(i,j,t)=\exp(\boldsymbol{Q}t)_{ij}.$$\end{document}

The probability of a set of observed walks x={x0,x1,...,xW}\begin{document}$x=\{x_{0},x_{1},...,x_{W}\}$\end{document}, where each walk contains a sequence of labelled steps xw={xw0,xw1,...,xwN}\begin{document}$x_{w}=\{x_{w0},x_{w1},...,x_{wN}\}$\end{document}, given a particular set of rate parameters Q is(5)P(x|Q)=∏w=0W∏n=0N−1p(xwn,xw(n+1),t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle P(x|\boldsymbol{Q})=\prod_{w=0}^{W}\prod_{n=0}^{N-1}p(x_{wn},x_{w(n+1)},t),$$\end{document}

where w and n are walk and step indices, respectively. We assume t=1\begin{document}$t=1$\end{document} for every step, as over the course of the entire random walk, the average step size in parameter space will be approximately constant.

Rates were inferred from the random walk simulation data by sampling the posterior distribution of Q using MCMC, implemented with the emcee package for Python (Foreman-Mackey et al., 2013). We ran 24 chains for 5000 steps with uniform priors between 0 and 0.1 for all transition rates. The first 2500 steps from each chain were discarded and the remaining part thinned by removing all but every 10th step to obtain the posterior distribution (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2). We took the mean of the posterior for each transition as the estimate for each transition rate in Figure 1. As an additional check, we also inferred the rates via maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) and found that they converged with the MCMC estimates (Appendix 1—figure 1A and B).

Because the inferred rates depend on the unit of time, we needed to normalise the transition rates to compare with the rates inferred from phylogeny. We did this for each mutational scheme by dividing by the mean of all transition rate estimates qij\begin{document}$q_{ij}$\end{document}. We define a normalised rate as(6)q^ij=qijq¯,q¯=112∑i,j∈{u,l,d,c}i≠jqij.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{q}_{ij} &= \frac{q_{ij}}{\bar{q}}, \\ \bar{q} &= \frac{1}{12} \sum_{\substack{i,j \in \{u,l,d,c\} \\ i \ne j}} q_{ij}. $$\end{document}

sec.title: Inferring evolutionary rates from phylogeny
sec.p: Although Geeta et al., 2012 had already inferred rates between these 4 categories with a phylogeny of 561 taxa, we wanted to test how robust these results are. Those results used a phylogeny that is now more than 25 years old (Soltis, 2000), and there are now much larger (e.g. Zuntini et al., 2024—9506 species) and more reliable phylogenies available. To do this analysis, we combined two phylogenetic trees (Janssens et al., 2020; Zuntini et al., 2024) with leaf images from the Naturalis herbarium (Naturalis Biodiversity Center, 2024). We first filtered all digitised records to just those from angiosperm families as per APG IV (The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, 2016). We then removed all but the first record for each species.

To see how the rates are affected by looking at the species-level versus the genus-level, we generated two trees for each original tree, one with species at the tips and one with all but one tip per genus removed. For the species-level trees, we took the intersection between the filtered herbarium data and the full trees. If more than 3100 tips remained, we sampled at random 3100 tips, to allow for manual classification within reasonable time limits. This gave a combined set of 5552 leaf images to classify for both species trees. Notably, the intersection between the herbarium data and the Zuntini et al., 2024 species tree gave 3057 taxa. Since this was less than 3100, no further sub-sampling was required, and so unlike all the other trees in this analysis, the Zuntini et al., 2024 species tree represents the raw intersection between the original tree and the herbarium. For this phylogeny, our genus tree and our species tree should both have similar levels of reliability. For the Janssens et al., 2020 phylogeny, we trust the genus-level tree more than the species-level tree, because the overlap with the herbarium data was not as good at the species-level. For example, taxa were more heavily concentrated in a smaller number of angiosperm families, compared to the other trees (Appendix 3—figure 1). Moreover, we sub-sampled down to 3100 taxa from 16,436 in the raw intersection to make manual classification feasible—something not required for the other trees.

For the genus-level trees, we further sub-sampled the angiosperm filtered herbarium data to 200 records per family, or the maximum if fewer than 200 records were present. The purpose of this step was to sample more evenly over phylogeny, accounting for potential biases in the herbarium. We then took the intersection between genera in this sample and each of our phylogenies and randomly selected one species from within each genus that was present in the herbarium to use as the label. This gave a combined set of 3359 leaf images to classify across both genus trees.

These images were then used to classify each species as one of the four categories (unlobed, lobed, dissected, or compound) or ambiguous. This was done by eye, relying on a sample of model leaves and their morphometric classifier output for reference (Figure 1B and Appendix 2—figure 6). After classification, all species labelled as ambiguous were removed, leaving an unambiguously labelled phylogeny (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1–5).

sec.p: We used 3 different phylogenies from the literature to infer the evolutionary rates. First, to compare our predictions directly to the Geeta et al., 2012 study, we used the same phylogeny as in their analysis (Soltis, 2000), which is based on 3 genes: nuclear 18S rDNA and the plastid genes rbcL and atpB. Second, we used a tree by Janssens et al., 2020, inferred using the plastid genes rbcL and matK (including trnK) and calibrated with 56 fossils. This tree comprises 36,101 species, representing 8399 genera, 426 families and all orders of flowering plants (available in Supplementary material 5 of Janssens et al., 2020). Finally, we used a recent phylogeny by Zuntini et al., 2024, containing 9506 species (7923 genera and all angiosperm families and orders), inferred using 353 nuclear genes and calibrated with 200 fossil records (available at https://zenodo.org/records/10778207; we used the tree 4-young-tree-smoothing-10-pruned-for-diversification-analyses). We show results from the Geeta et al., 2012 phylogeny, labelled with their own classification data and the Janssens et al., 2020 and Zuntini et al., 2024 trees labelled with our own classification data from Naturalis Biodiversity Center, 2024.

Rates were inferred using the MultiState method from BayesTraits V4.1.2 (Pagel et al., 2004). We used MCMC for 1,100,000 iterations with a sample period of 1000 and removed the first 100,000 iterations to obtain posterior distributions. We used a uniform prior between 0 and 0.1 for the Zuntini et al., 2024 trees (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4) and Janssens et al., 2020 trees (Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6). However, for the Geeta et al., 2012 tree, because branch lengths are measured in substitutions per site rather than millions of years, we instead used a uniform prior between 0 and 100 (Figure 3—figure supplement 7). We took the mean of each posterior as the transition rate estimate. In addition, we estimated the rates using MLE for comparison (Appendix 1—figure 1A and B). As the units of time differ between our phylogenies and the simulations, we needed to normalise the rates to allow for comparison. We did this using the same method as for the simulations (Equation 6): by dividing each transition rate estimate by the mean transition rate estimate for each tree.

sec.title: Leaf model details
sec.p: In this section, we provide a more detailed overview of how model parameters relate to growth processes. For further model details, please also see the main text and supplementary information of Runions et al., 2017.

sec.title: Initialisation

caption.title: The initial leaf ‘primordium’ at the start of the simulation labelled with a selection of initialisation parameters.
caption.p: Parameters I0–I12 specify which compounds/morphogens are present at each sample point, in this case either compound 0, 1 or 2. I_SAMPDIST specifies the vertical distance between sample points and NSAMP gives the total primordium length in number of sample points.

sec.p: The initial condition of the Runions et al., 2017 simulation is a primordium (Appendix 2—figure 1) with user-defined dimensions and morphogen distribution along the margin. These properties are specified by the following initialisation parameters.

list-item.p: NSAMP – primordium length in number of sample points.
I_SAMPDIST – vertical distance between sample points.
INITSTATE – an array containing I0–I12. Specifies which compounds are present at each sample point in the primordium.
PRIMSCALEX – the primordium is scaled in x according to this value.
PRIMSCALEY – the primordium is scaled in y according to this value.

sec.title: Margin webbing

caption.title: Stronger webbing results in shallower lobes.
caption.p: Stronger webbing results in faster growth of the margin and lamina between vein tips (convergence points) to reduce stretching. The overall rate of webbing depends on multiple morphogen-associated model parameters. In this example, compound 2 (dark blue) has stronger webbing for the right-hand leaf, resulting in faster growth in the lobes where it is localised.

sec.p: The margin parameters control patterning, webbing and tip growth. Patterning is the addition of new vein tips (convergence points) and the updating of compound positions. Webbing is the rate at which the margin deforms to reduce stretching and bending. Tip growth is the rate of extension of vein tips.

Webbing (Appendix 2—figure 2) is simulated for each sample point Pi\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_i}$\end{document} along the leaf margin that is not a vein tip/convergence point, where i is the sample point index. It is implemented as a displacement vector ΔWi\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{W_i}$\end{document} that is calculated as the weighted sum of 4 other displacement vectors: stretch (ΔSi\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{S_i}$\end{document}), curvature 1 (ΔKi(1)\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(1)}_i}$\end{document}), curvature 2 (ΔKi(2)\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(2)}_i}$\end{document}), and normal displacement (Ni\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{N_i}$\end{document}).(2.1)ΔWi=αSΔSi+αK(1)ΔKi(1)+αK(2)ΔKi(2)+αNNi\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta \boldsymbol{W_i} = \alpha_S \Delta \boldsymbol{S_i} + \alpha_{K^{(1)}} \Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(1)}_i} + \alpha_{K^{(2)}} \Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(2)}_i} + \alpha_N \boldsymbol{N_i}$$\end{document}

Each of these vectors is weighted by user-controlled parameters αS\begin{document}$\alpha_S$\end{document}, αK(1)\begin{document}$\alpha_{K^{(1)}}$\end{document}, αK(2)\begin{document}$\alpha_{K^{(2)}}$\end{document} and αN\begin{document}$\alpha_N$\end{document}. The first three vectors (ΔSi\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{S_i}$\end{document}, ΔKi(1)\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(1)}_i}$\end{document}, ΔKi(2)\begin{document}$\Delta \boldsymbol{K^{(2)}_i}$\end{document}) are calculated by minimising an energy term for all sample points in the margin P0,P1,...,Pn\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_0}, \boldsymbol{P_1},..., \boldsymbol{P_n}$\end{document}.

The stretch energy ES\begin{document}$E_S$\end{document} is given by(2.2)ES=∑i=1n||Pi−Pi−1||2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle E_S=\sum^{n}_{i=1}||\boldsymbol{P_i} - \boldsymbol{P_{i-1}}||^2.$$\end{document}

Curvature is approximated using two different expressions for additional flexibility. The first curvature energy is approximated for each sample point by the turning angle θi\begin{document}$\theta_i$\end{document}. So for the entire margin this results in the curvature energy(2.3)EK(1)=∑i=1n−1θi2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle E_{K^{(1)}} = \sum^{n-1}_{i=1} \theta^2_i.$$\end{document}

The second curvature energy is given by the weighted second finite difference about each sample point(2.4)EK(2)=∑i=1n−1||wliPi−1−wciPi+wriPi+1||2,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle E_{K^{(2)}} = \sum^{n-1}_{i=1} ||w^i_l \boldsymbol{P_{i-1}} - w^i_c \boldsymbol{P_i} + w^i_r \boldsymbol{P_{i+1}}||^2,$$\end{document}

where wli=wri=12\begin{document}$w^i_l = w^i_r = \frac{1}{2}$\end{document} and wci=1\begin{document}$w^i_c = 1$\end{document}. These weights result in a vector from Pi\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_i}$\end{document} to the mid-point of the line between Pi−1\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_{i-1}}$\end{document} and Pi+1\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_{i+1}}$\end{document}.

Finally the magnitude of the normal displacement vector for each sample point Pi\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{P_i}$\end{document} is proportional to the average length of the adjacent margin edges(2.5)12(||Pi+1−Pi||+||Pi−Pi−1||).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\big(||\boldsymbol{P_{i+1}} - \boldsymbol{P_i}|| + ||\boldsymbol{P_i} - \boldsymbol{P_{i-1}}||\big).$$\end{document}

To calculate the overall webbing vector for each sample point, each of these terms is weighted by a user-controlled parameter: stretch (αS\begin{document}$\alpha_S$\end{document}) - STRETCH, curvature 1 (αK(1)\begin{document}$\alpha_{K^{(1)}}$\end{document}) - CFLOW, curvature 2 (αK(2)\begin{document}$\alpha_{K^{(2)}}$\end{document}) - CURVATURE, normal displacement (αN\begin{document}$\alpha_N$\end{document}) - NORMAL.

Many margin parameters are associated with particular morphogens/compounds and have the name format <parameter_name><morphogen_number>, e.g. FAIRING2. For a particular margin segment, not all margin parameters are necessarily used, as the parameters used depend on the compounds present there. If there are 2 compounds present, each will have its own set of parameters actively playing a role in growth and form. Webbing can be controlled by the user via the following parameters.

list-item.p: TIP_GROWTH – controls the rate at which vein tips are displaced in the vein direction.
FAIRING – controls the total rate of webbing.
CURVATURE – controls the rate of bending.
CFLOW – controls the rate of bending.
STRETCH – controls the distance between neighbouring margin points.
NORMAL – the amount that margin points are displaced normal to the curve.

sec.title: Margin patterning

caption.title: Margins are patterned by convergence points and morphogens/compounds.
caption.p: New convergence points are inserted between existing convergence points, where the intervening distance along the margin exceeds a threshold value. Compounds/morphogens on the margin can alter the measured distances between convergence points, affecting where new convergence points are inserted. New veins are inserted to connect new convergence points to the existing vasculature, thereby specifying new growth axes. Compounds can also alter the rate of webbing between veins.

sec.p: The margin is patterned by convergence points, which mark the tips of new veins, and compounds (also referred to as morphogens) (Appendix 2—figure 3). The patterning process occurs by first measuring distances along the margin. This informs where convergence points and thus veins should be added. The margin points at which compounds are expressed are updated in response to the new convergence points. Finally, new veins are added to connect the convergence points to the existing vasculature.
The following parameters control margin patterning globally.

list-item.p: LASSYMETRY – the distance value on the first (left) point along the margin. Can be thought of as the effect of neighbouring tissue on the leaf primordium.
RASSYMETRY – the distance value on the last (right) point along the margin.
INTERVAL – the distance along the margin between two convergence points over which a compound will be expressed.

sec.p: The following parameters have compound-specific effects.

list-item.p: METRIC – the rate at which distances along the margin increase relative to arc-length distances. Measured distances can increase more slowly or more rapidly than the arc-length distance as the leaf grows depending on the value here.
CPDIST – new convergence points are added to a margin segment when the distance measured along this segment exceeds this value. This may differ between compounds.
PATTERNABLE – controls whether margin segments expressing this compound are competent for new convergence points.
COMPETENCE – sets the maximum distance from the leaf base a margin segment can be and still be competent for new convergence points.
COMPETENCET – maximum time step beyond which a margin segment will no longer be competent for new convergence points.
EXTENDABLE – whether the interval in which a compound is expressed can increase in size or not.
EXTENDABLE_CONTEXT – which compounds can be overwritten. When a compound number is greater than this value, it can be overwritten.

sec.title: Vein patterning

caption.title: New veins attach to existing vasculature at angle θ.
caption.p: Attachment is restricted such that the angle made with the margin σ cannot exceed σmax\begin{document}$\sigma_{\max}$\end{document}. Veins attach so as to minimise ‘resistance’—the total distance from the vein tip to either the base of the leaf or the existing vasculature, depending on the value of GLOBAL_RESISTANCE.

sec.p: New veins attach convergence points to existing vasculature so as to minimise resistance (Appendix 2—figure 4). Resistance depends on the distance travelled in the blade and the distance travelled in the vasculature to the leaf base. The user can exert some control over vein attachment through the following parameters.

list-item.p: AXISANGLE – the angle at which new veins branch from existing veins.
MAXANGLE – the maximum angle veins can make with the margin. This restricts the orientation of new veins.

GLOBAL_RESISTANCE – determines how the resistance (length) of veins affects where a vein will join to the existing vasculature. A value of 0 means only the resistance of the new vein segment is considered. A value of 1 means the total resistance of the entire path to the leaf base is considered.

sec.title: Global growth

caption.title: Veins are the main axes of growth, pushing the local margin outwards in successive time points.
caption.p: The rate of growth of the veins and margin depends on the distance to the base of the leaf. Growth of veins and margin is fastest near the base of the leaf, tailing off towards the tip depending on the values of parameters such as VG_START_X for vein growth.

sec.p: Growth is a combination of uniform scaling, vein tip displacement, webbing and vein extension. The global rate of tip displacement, webbing and vein extension depends on the distance to the leaf base as measured along the veins according to a growth gradient (Appendix 2—figure 5). Vein growth rate can also be age-dependent.

list-item.p: UNIFORM_GROWTH – the rate of uniform scaling.
TG_START_X – the distance from the leaf base along the veins that the rate of tip growth begins to decrease.
TG_END_X – the distance from the leaf base along the veins that the rate of tip growth reaches its minimum.
FG_START_X – the distance from the leaf base that the rate of webbing growth begins to fall off.
FG_END_X – the distance from the leaf base that the rate of webbing growth stops decreasing.
VG_GRATE – base vein growth rate.
VG_START_X – distance from leaf base that the rate of vein growth begins to fall off.
VG_END_X – distance from leaf base that the rate of vein growth stops decreasing.
CP_AD_TIP_GROWTH – rate of extra early tip growth.
CP_ADTG_FALLOFF – time period over which early growth disappears.
AX_AD_AXIS_GROWTH – rate of extra early vein-extension.
AX_ADAG_FALLOFF – time period over which early vein extension growth disappears.
APEX_TIP_GROWTH – extra tip growth for the primary axis.
ASYMMETRIC_FAIRING – whether the rate of webbing can be different on either side of a convergence point.
ASYMM_PRE – the rate of webbing before the convergence point.
ASYMM_POST – the rate of webbing after the convergence point.
SHARP_LEAF_TIP – whether to disable webbing at the leaf tip.
INTERNAL_FLOW – whether webbing can only occur in the outward direction.
PETIOLE_COMPOUND – the compound which specifies the petiole.
PETIOLE_EXTEND – whether the petiole (as marked by PETIOLE_COMPOUND) is enlarged by uniform growth.

sec.title: Phylogenetic rate inference
sec.p: We use the MultiState method from BayesTraits V4 to infer transition rates from phylogenetic data. MultiState fits a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to a discrete character distributed across the tips of a phylogeny. The tree topology and character states at the tips are fixed, with only the CTMC parameters defined by the matrix Q being estimated.

The optimal Q is found by maximising the likelihood L of the observed tip data D given the phylogenetic tree T (topology and branch lengths) and the value of Q (Pagel, 1994). Let T=(V,E)\begin{document}$T = (V, E)$\end{document} denote the tree, with leaf nodes Vtip⊂V\begin{document}$V_{\text{tip}} \subset V$\end{document} which have observed states Dv\begin{document}$D_v$\end{document} for v∈Vtip\begin{document}$v \in V_{\text{tip}}$\end{document}, and internal nodes Vint=V∖Vtip\begin{document}$V_{\text{int}} = V \setminus V_{\text{tip}}$\end{document} (including the root) which have unobserved states. Under the assumptions of the CTMC, the probability of a single branch (u,v)∈E\begin{document}$(u,v) \in E$\end{document} with parent state xu\begin{document}$x_u$\end{document}, child state xv\begin{document}$x_v$\end{document} and branch length tuv\begin{document}$t_{uv}$\end{document} is(3.1)p(xu,xv,tuv)=[exp⁡(Qtuv)]xuxv\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p(x_u,x_v,t_{uv}) = \big[\exp(\boldsymbol{Q}t_{uv})\big]_{x_ux_v}$$\end{document}

The likelihood is then the product of the probabilities for all branches in the tree summed over all possible assignments of character states at internal nodes (Pagel, 1994).(3.2)L(D|Q,T)=∑{xv}v∈Vint∏(u,v)∈Ep(xu,xv,tuv).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle L(D | \boldsymbol{Q}, T) = \sum_{\{x_v\}_{v \in V_\text{int}}} \prod_{(u,v) \in E}p(x_u,x_v,t_{uv}).$$\end{document}

The pruning algorithm (Felsenstein, 1981) is used to compute this likelihood more efficiently. The likelihood surface for Q is then searched, in the case of MLE, to find the value of Q that gives the maximum likelihood solution via the BOBYQA algorithm (Meade and Pagel, 2024). In the case of MCMC, a posterior distribution is sampled using Metropolis-Hastings (Pagel et al., 2004). This posterior is given by(3.3)p(Q|D,T)=p(D|Q,T)p(Q)∫Qp(D|Q,T)p(Q)dQ\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{Q} | D, T) = \frac{p(D | \boldsymbol{Q}, T) p(\boldsymbol{Q})} {\int_{\boldsymbol{Q}} p(D | \boldsymbol{Q}, T) p(\boldsymbol{Q})d\boldsymbol{Q}}$$\end{document}

where p(D|Q,T)=L(D|Q,T)\begin{document}$p(D | \boldsymbol{Q}, T) = L(D | \boldsymbol{Q}, T)$\end{document}, p(Q)\begin{document}$p(\boldsymbol{Q})$\end{document} is the prior distribution and the denominator integrates over all possible values of Q. We use uniform priors between 0 and 0.1 for all trees except Geeta et al., 2012 for which we use a uniform prior between 0 and 100. This is because branch lengths for Geeta et al., 2012 are measured in substitutions per site rather than millions of years.
All non-diagonal elements of Q are permitted to vary freely during the fitting process. Diagonal elements are set to the negative sum of other elements in the same row, such that rows sum to zero.

Elements qij\begin{document}$q_{ij}$\end{document} of Q represent the instantaneous rate of transition between state i and j in units of transitions per unit of branch length. To allow comparison between phylogenies with different branch lengths, we normalise the Q matrix for each tree by dividing each transition rate by the mean of the off-diagonal elements of Q (Methods: Inferring evolutionary rates from phylogeny).
