sec.title: A short literature review of the adaptive significance of leaf shape
Introduction
sec.p: As the primary sites of photosynthesis, leaves are critical to plant fitness. They also display extraordinary variation in shape. It is therefore natural to ask to what extent this variation is the product of natural selection. Functional properties of leaves where shape may be relevant include thermoregulation, hydraulic efficiency, biomechanical stability, herbivory defence, light interception and nutrient cycling. Yet, despite an extensive and sophisticated literature, the extent to which leaf shape determines fitness, and hence reflects adaptation, remains the subject of considerable debate. In particular, a recurring difficulty in this literature is distinguishing evidence that morphology affects leaf function from evidence that the resulting functional differences affect fitness, and ultimately from evidence that selection on those differences explains evolutionary patterns of leaf shape.

In this short overview we briefly survey the literature on the role of adaptation in shaping three different classes of shape variables. The first is leaf size, which can vary enormously, from less than 1mm2\begin{document}$1\,\text{mm}^2$\end{document} to over 1m2\begin{document}$1\,\text{m}^2$\end{document}, and correlates quite strongly with climate: it was noted more than a century ago that leaves tend to be large in hot, sunny and wet climates, and small in hot, sunny and arid climates. The second class is marginal leaf teeth, which are small oscillatory patterns or serrations on the margin of leaves. The presence and number of teeth are thought to correlate with mean annual temperature, and have historically been used as a proxy to infer paleoclimate trends. The main class we treat here comprises dissection traits, which are captured by our unlobed, lobed, dissected and compound categories. We note that each of these four dissection categories can exhibit large variations in size, and can be toothed or untoothed.

sec.title: Size
sec.p: Leaf size is thought to be particularly important for thermoregulation, hydraulic performance, and light capture. In the case of thermoregulation, leaves need to regulate their temperature to maintain efficient photosynthesis and respiration, prevent damage from heat stress and freezing, and balance heat loss against water loss through transpiration (Berry and Bjorkman, 1980; Givnish, 1987; Wright et al., 2017; Perez and Feeley, 2020). Heat exchange between a leaf and the surrounding air depends partly on the thickness of the boundary layer of relatively still air at the leaf surface (Vogel, 1970). Smaller leaves generally have thinner boundary layers and therefore exchange heat with the surrounding air more rapidly than larger leaves. A recent large-scale study which analysed 7670 species from 682 sites worldwide (Wright et al., 2017) argued that the leaf-to-air temperature difference plays a key role in explaining why large leaves predominate in warm, wet environments, whereas small leaves are common in hot, arid environments and at high altitudes. Interestingly, although these authors did separate out simple from compound leaf shapes, both dissection categories showed similar trends with climate variables.

Leaf size may also influence hydraulic performance. For example, Scoffoni et al., 2011 used simulations and comparisons among 10 species with different drought tolerance to show that smaller leaves with greater major-vein density showed reduced hydraulic vulnerability and greater tolerance to vein embolism. Thus, variation in size may influence both the thermal and hydraulic conditions under which leaves can function. See also Sack and Scoffoni, 2013.

Size is also associated with trade-offs in light capture and resource allocation. Increasing leaf area can increase total photosynthetic surface (Watson, 1958), but leaf mass increases with area while proportional gains in area diminish, implying increasing construction costs for larger leaves (Niklas et al., 2007). Leaf size additionally interacts with canopy architecture. Smaller leaves may be associated with shorter petioles and greater crowding around stems, potentially increasing self-shading (Falster and Westoby, 2003). The leaf economic spectrum further demonstrates that investment in leaf structure is associated with major differences in leaf lifespan and photosynthetic return (Wright et al., 2004).

In conclusion, leaf size can have substantial functional consequences and is likely shaped by trade-offs between heat exchange, hydraulic efficiency, construction costs, and light capture. The evidence linking leaf size to ecologically important functions and environmental gradients is arguably stronger than the corresponding evidence for many aspects of leaf shape. Many of the functions affected by leaf size can also be modified by other aspects of leaf shape. This makes disentangling adaptive from non-adaptive variation more complex.

sec.title: Teeth
sec.p: Marginal teeth are shallow projections or serrations separated by sinuses, incised less than 25% of the distance to the midvein (Ellis et al., 2009). They are a much less pronounced feature than our dissection categories. Unlobed, lobed, dissected leaves, as well as the leaflets of compound leaves, can be either toothed or untoothed. Indeed, a close look at the first two unlobed leaves in Appendix 2—figure 6 reveals a toothed pattern in one and an untoothed pattern in the other, illustrating that the Runions model (Runions et al., 2017) can reproduce this feature on top of the dissection traits.

The presence or absence of leaf teeth has been of particular interest for over a century, due to an observed negative correlation with mean annual temperature (MAT), in particular for woody dicot species (Bailey and Sinnott, 1916). The association between climate and leaf tooth presence has been measured repeatedly (Bailey and Sinnott, 1916; Royer et al., 2005; Peppe et al., 2011), including by a study across 3549 species and 6 continents (Royer et al., 2012). The apparent simplicity and strength of this relationship led to its widespread use to estimate paleoclimate MAT. However, as independent methods for reconstructing past temperatures such as oxygen-isotope measurements and phytoplankton distributions were refined and recalibrated, discrepancies began to emerge between estimates of MAT based on fossil leaf margins and those obtained from these independent paleoclimate proxies. This motivated work to better understand and refine the relationship (Burnham and Tonkovich, 2011). Multivariate approaches, particularly Climate-Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP) (Wolfe, 1993) or digital leaf physiognomy (Peppe et al., 2011), were subsequently developed and refined to incorporate additional aspects of leaf morphology (Wolfe, 1993; Peppe et al., 2011). New features, including the shape factor (4π×blade area/perimeter2\begin{document}$4\pi \times \text{blade area}/\text{perimeter}^2$\end{document}), a measure of roundness, were found to correlate with MAT, albeit with a modest amount of variance explained (r2=0.22,P<0.001\begin{document}$r^2=0.22, P \lt 0.001$\end{document}) (Peppe et al., 2011).

However, there are several complicating factors. An important study of 569 species-site pairs that explicitly took phylogenetic models into account demonstrated that ancestry of plant species also plays a significant role in all 21 leaf traits measured, including the abundance of teeth (Little et al., 2010). Accounting for shared ancestry decreased the slope of the regression between the presence of teeth and mean annual temperature by an order of magnitude (in log space) to almost a flat line with wider confidence intervals. This suggests that the geographical correlation contains a substantial phylogenetic component, although it does not by itself distinguish whether this arises from phylogenetic constraint, climatic sorting of lineages, or repeated adaptive convergent evolution of toothed or untoothed margins. Subsequent studies suggest that an association between temperature and tooth presence remains after accounting for phylogeny, potentially mediated by venation architecture (Zohner et al., 2019), although the picture remains complex (Li et al., 2016), and clear counterexamples to the MAT correlation with teeth can also be found in certain species (Burnham and Tonkovich, 2011; Frye et al., 2020).

Interestingly, Little et al., 2010 also found that relationships between MAT and more gross shape variables such as shape factor changed little after phylogenetic correction, making these associations more consistent with repeated environmental responses across lineages. However, these correlations are not that strong in the first place. Moreover, the shape factor captures roundness rather than the specific distinctions among unlobed, lobed, dissected, and compound leaves we consider in this study. Overall, an emerging consensus in the field is that evolutionary history and climatic selection jointly contribute to the observed relationship rather than that the relationship is simply a phylogenetic artefact. Modern work on paleoenvironmental reconstruction combines different leaf shape traits with phylogenetic, biogeographic and other analyses rather than relying on the fraction of leaves with teeth alone.

Despite the complications above, many functional hypotheses have been proposed to explain the climate association. Firstly, enhanced early-season photosynthesis at leaf teeth could be particularly advantageous in climates with short growing seasons (Royer and Wilf, 2006). Secondly, the ‘support-supply’ hypothesis posits that cooler climates with short growing seasons favour thinner leaves with stronger veins that penetrate to the margin for which the optimal shape of the surrounding tissue is wedge-like (Givnish and Kriebel, 2017). Thirdly, the ‘bud-packing’ hypothesis postulates that cold climates favour dense packing of leaf primordia in buds which results in more teeth due to physical forces from folding (Edwards et al., 2016). However, the evidence for these is mixed. Although Royer and Wilf, 2006 show enhanced photosynthesis and transpiration in toothed margins early in the growing season, the extent to which this increases fitness is unclear. Moreover, Zohner et al., 2019 found that leaf thickness does not predict venation and teeth, contradicting the support-supply hypothesis. They also found that primordium number in buds does not predict margin state, contradicting the bud-packing hypothesis.

In summary, several explanations for the correlation between leaf teeth and MAT remain viable. Teeth may be direct targets of selection because of some functional property they confer, but the relationship could also arise from a more complex combination of adaptive effects, including effects that partly cancel one another or from relatively weak selection. Alternatively, the association between leaf teeth and climate may arise indirectly through selection on other aspects of leaf function. Thus, even for leaf toothiness, where the geographical association with climate is unusually strong and well replicated, identifying the selective mechanism responsible for that association remains difficult. This provides a useful point of comparison for the more pronounced dissection traits considered below, for which geographical correlations are generally less well established.

sec.title: Dissection and compoundness
sec.p: In this section we look in more detail at the literature linking leaf dissection traits, measured in our case through the lobed, unlobed, dissected and compound leaf shapes, to a series of different functions of leaves.

sec.title: Thermoregulation
sec.p: Thermoregulation is frequently proposed as an important driver of leaf-shape evolution (Nicotra et al., 2011). In particular, complex leaves have been hypothesised to behave aerodynamically like many small leaves, resulting in faster heat transfer to the environment (Leigh et al., 2017). Laboratory studies using artificial leaves have suggested that leaf heat exchange with the environment is strongly influenced by shape (Vogel, 1970). For example, Vogel, 1970 found that lobed copper plates were more effective heat dissipators than circles. However, this approach ignores other important traits of real leaves (e.g. water content, absorptance) that have large effects on the actual operating temperatures of leaves in natural environments (Nicotra et al., 2011).

A more recent study by Leigh et al., 2017 measured multiple temperature variables in field conditions for 68 Proteaceae species, finding that effective leaf width was a strong predictor of leaf thermal dynamics, whereas leaf margin complexity had no or weak effects. Thus, although dissection can affect convective heat transfer under controlled conditions, its contribution to leaf temperature in vivo may be small relative to other morphological and physiological traits.

Ivyleaf morning glory (Ipomoea hederacea) provides an unusually well-studied test case. An investigation of lobed and unlobed genotypes of Ipomoea hederacea (Singhal et al., 2025) revealed that while both shapes maintain similar temperatures, unlobed phenotypes had significantly increased stomatal conductance in warmer, sunnier conditions. This suggests that unlobed leaves may rely more on latent cooling via transpiration for temperature regulation compared to lobed leaves. The fact that lobed leaves maintain the same temperature without increased stomatal conductance is consistent with a different cooling strategy, perhaps enhanced convective cooling facilitated by the lobed shape to conserve water. This highlights how thermoregulation depends on a range of traits and even if leaf shape is one of them, suboptimal leaf shapes can arise due to trade-offs with these other traits.

Ipomoea hederacea also provides an instructive example of the difficulty of inferring selection from geographical patterns. The species has a clear latitudinal cline in North America, from lobed genotypes in the north to heart-shaped unlobed genotypes in the south, that is known to be determined by a single locus (Campitelli and Stinchcombe, 2013a). Campitelli and Stinchcombe, 2013a showed that the leaf shape locus displays clinal variation and neutral loci do not, consistent with the leaf shape cline being caused by selection on leaf shape. However, it is possible that selection is acting instead on a different locus in linkage disequilibrium with the leaf shape locus. They suggest that the agent of selection could be temperature. However, contrary to previous studies that predict that lobes are favoured in hot environments, the lobed genotypes are found more frequently in the colder north end of the cline. To identify the selective agent for this cline, Campitelli and Stinchcombe, 2013b planted 1680 lobed-unlobed F3 hybrids with varying leaf shape in the north and measured their fitness as well as other selective agents including temperature and herbivory. They found that none of the potential selective agents affected the different leaf shape genotypes differently. This could be because the true selective agent was not among those investigated, or that the cline is not due to selection on leaf shape but is perhaps instead due to selection on another trait in linkage disequilibrium. This study highlights the difficulty in establishing selection as a cause, despite correlations between leaf shape and environmental variables.

sec.title: Hydraulic efficiency
sec.p: Leaf shape has also been proposed to influence hydraulic efficiency. Photosynthetic capacity is directly impacted by the efficiency of water transport through leaves, which alone accounts for ≥30%\begin{document}$\geq30\%$\end{document} of the total resistance to water flow through plants (Sack and Frole, 2006). Leaf structure, particularly venation architecture, strongly affects the strength of this resistance.

Sisó et al., 2001 found that in seven species of oak (Quercus), leaves with increased lobation had lower hydraulic resistance. It is thought that this is caused by a lower ratio of mesophyll tissue to vasculature in lobed leaves. This is consistent with the hypothesis that deeply lobed leaves may be a way of improving water balance in arid environments.

On the other hand, Sack and Frole, 2006 investigated the relationship between leaf structure and hydraulic resistance in 10 coexisting tropical rain forest tree species in Panama. They found that while resistance was negatively associated with vein density, there was no significant association with shape. Moreover, Scoffoni et al., 2011 found, through simulations and comparisons among 10 diverse species with highly varying drought tolerance, that smaller leaves with higher major vein density had reduced hydraulic vulnerability and higher tolerance to vein embolism (the blocking of veins by air bubbles).
Therefore, while shape may have some effect on hydraulic efficiency, properties of the vasculature, such as vein density, may more directly determine hydraulic function.

sec.title: Biomechanical stability
sec.p: Leaves are constantly subjected to various mechanical stresses from their environment, including static loads such as their own weight, accumulated snow or ice, and dynamic loads primarily from wind and rain. In order to maintain optimal fitness-critical functions such as photosynthesis, they need to withstand these stresses with minimal damage and maintain optimal positioning for light interception. Much of the biomechanical literature concerns dimensions or petiole properties rather than dissection per se. However, it is possible that leaf shape affects the ability to withstand mechanical stress and therefore has been optimised by natural selection for mechanical robustness, particularly in high-stress environments (e.g. windy environments).

Tadrist and Darbois-Texier, 2016 found that they could predict scaling relationships among palm leaf length, width, thickness and petiole diameter with a mathematical model that maximises surface area under gravitational self-support constraints. This suggests that for this particular group of large-leaved plants, leaf dimensions may be constrained by optimisation for self-support. It is not clear how important other shape features, such as margin complexity, are for self-support.

Moreover, Louf et al., 2018 predicted a relationship between blade aspect ratio and the relative bending and twisting rigidity of petioles, which was broadly consistent with measurements from four broad-leaved species. This is consistent with adaptive trade-offs between leaf shape and petiole mechanical properties as a result of mechanical stress from wind.

Niklas, 1996 found that leaves from wind-exposed and protected sugar maple trees (Acer saccharum) differed significantly in some aspects of shape. Leaves from wind-exposed trees had smaller surface areas and shorter and narrower petioles that were less rigid than petioles from leaves on protected trees. These differences are thought to be due to adaptive phenotypic plasticity in response to chronic mechanical perturbation by wind. The shorter, more flexible petioles allow for easier twisting and bending in response to the wind, reducing drag forces and the chance of mechanical tissue damage (Niklas, 1999).

Different leaf shapes experience different levels of drag, relative to their surface area, in response to wind. Through wind-tunnel experiments, Vogel, 1989 found that pinnately compound leaves had lower drag than clusters of simple leaves by reconfiguring into a streamlined cylinder shape with alternately layered leaflets. This demonstrates a physical effect of leaf shape on drag and reconfiguration in wind, although whether this translates into differences in fitness remains to be established.

sec.title: Herbivory defence
sec.p: Leaf herbivory is costly to plant fitness by reducing photosynthetic capacity. Leaves have evolved many features that deter herbivores such as chemical toxicity and physical barriers such as the waxy cuticle, thorns and trichomes. The role of leaf shape is less obvious; nevertheless, there is some evidence that it can impact herbivory.

For example, Higuchi and Kawakita, 2019 showed that the leaf-rolling weevil Apoderus praecellens could be deterred from cutting the leaves of its host genus Isodon by replacing leaves from an unlobed species (I. trichocarpus) typical of the genus with lobed leaves from a closely related species (I. umbrosus). They controlled for potential confounding differences between the plant species by cutting lobes into I. trichocarpus leaves to resemble I. umbrosus, and still found a preference for the unlobed I. trichocarpus leaves among the female weevils.

Moreover, there is observational (Rausher, 1978) and direct experimental (Dell’Aglio et al., 2016) evidence that ovipositing butterflies use vision to recognise plant hosts by leaf shape and can have a preference for some shapes over others. This shows that butterflies have the potential to exert selection on leaf shape in host species.

On the other hand, Campitelli et al., 2008 investigated how alternative leaf morphs of the Ipomoea hederacea affect the performance (e.g. insect biomass, leaf area consumed, digestive efficiency) of three different generalist insect herbivores. They found that the effect of shape on performance was highly variable between insect species, plant developmental stage and growth conditions. Therefore, while some insect herbivores may be able to consume certain leaf shapes more easily, it seems there is no consistent trend and other plant traits may play a more significant role.

sec.title: Light interception and optimisation
sec.p: Leaves function as the primary organs for light harvesting in vascular plants and are therefore of utmost importance to photosynthetic capacity. While the effects of several non-shape traits on photosynthetic capacity are well understood, the effect of shape per se is more uncertain (Nicotra et al., 2011).

Simulations of maize (Zea mays) have found that variation in leaf shape can alter light interception by up to 7% (Otto et al., 2025). Z. mays leaves do not vary as substantially in shape as those of other lineages, suggesting that the effect on light interception may be greater for other plants with more shape variation.

Further simulations in oil palm found that parameters related to leaf area had the largest effect on light interception and carbon assimilation, and the effect of other shape parameters was less important (Perez et al., 2018).

Several studies on poplars have shown that some aspects of leaf shape can evolve to reduce self-shading within canopies. Aspen (Populus tremuloides) has evolved a flattened, non-rigid petiole oriented perpendicular to the leaf blade, resulting in enhanced leaf flutter even in light winds (Roden, 2003). By directly measuring light intensity at different points within the canopy of two poplar species, Roden and Pearcy, 1993a showed that leaf flutter increased light penetration into the lower canopy, creating a more spatially even understory light environment. This can enhance whole canopy carbon gain, as understory poplar leaves are very efficient at utilising rapidly fluctuating light environments for photosynthesis (Roden and Pearcy, 1993b). Furthermore, evidence from simulations suggests that fluttering leaves at the top of the canopy have more uniform light interception than static leaves and therefore also potentially enhanced carbon gain (Roden, 2003). This highlights how leaf shape can indirectly alter light interception by altering the mechanical response to wind. It is not clear how the shape of parts of the leaf besides the petiole could affect flutter.

Donoghue et al., 2022 identified a link between leaf morphology and light levels in geographically isolated populations of Viburnum in Mexican and South American cloud forests. These populations showed convergent evolution of different leaf ecomorphs, consistent with repeated adaptive evolution into the same niches across these isolated locations. However, the authors did not rule out neutral evolution as a potential cause. By measuring environmental variables in these isolated populations, they identified a positive correlation between large leaves, lower light levels and higher wetness. This is consistent with the hypothesis that larger leaves are an adaptation to lower light environments, but does not prove any differences in fitness associated with leaf shape. Moreover, the main correlation they found was related to size rather than shape.

sec.title: Nutrient cycling
sec.p: Deciduous trees shed their leaves annually, avoiding the cost of maintaining foliage under the stress of winter. However, this results in these trees losing 40% of their assimilated carbon and substantial amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients (Biviano and Jensen, 2025). Given the potential nutritional value of these leaves, it is possible that there is a fitness benefit to trees that deposit their leaves nearby, such that their nutrients can be recycled and local soil conditions are improved. Biviano and Jensen, 2025 investigated the hypothesis that symmetric and unlobed leaves may have evolved as a strategy to increase leaf settling speed such that fallen leaves land closer to the tree of origin, facilitating nutrient retention. Through experiments with paper leaves, they found that highly symmetric shapes settled the fastest, with increasing lobedness decreasing settling speed. Asymmetric shapes settled substantially more slowly and were largely insensitive to changes in lobedness. This is consistent with the notion that leaf shape may also be under selection to facilitate nutrient recycling by maximising settling speed.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: While the evidence for adaptation is much weaker for these dissection categories than it is for leaf size or even teeth, there remains substantial evidence that leaf dissection and compoundness can influence thermoregulation, hydraulics, mechanical behaviour, herbivore interactions and light interception. However, most studies establish functional effects rather than fitness consequences, and many are restricted to particular species or lineages. Moreover, in several cases leaf size, venation or petiole architecture appear to have stronger functional effects than dissection itself. Dissection may therefore be adaptive in particular ecological contexts, and different selective pressures may favour similar shapes in different contexts, but there is currently limited evidence for a general selective explanation for its broad evolutionary distribution. Absence of evidence is not necessarily evidence of absence. So, while there may still be an adaptive explanation, or several explanations, for the higher evolutionary transition rates towards unlobed shapes than complex shapes—lobed, dissected and compound—the current literature does not offer a clear answer to what this might be.

body.p: This paper presents important findings on how the shapes of leaves might be biased towards simpler shapes due to biases in how variation is generated by developmental processes rather than selection. The authors present convincing evidence that combines image analysis of a herbarium dataset and computational analysis of a model of leaf development. The paper should be of interest to diverse researchers, ranging from plant development to the evolution of complexity more broadly.

[Editors' note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]
Summary:

The authors aim to understand, in the context of leaf shape, how the constraints imposed by development inform evolution. Leaf shape is a good place to study the influence of development on evolution because it is a trait that exhibits a lot of diversity, and the developmental mechanisms that give rise to leaf shapes are apparently rather conserved across angiosperms.

As part of the motivation for their work, the authors cite a previous study (Geeta et al), which found that in angiosperm phylogenies, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes occur through evolution more often than transitions in the opposite direction. Is this due to developmental constraints or adaptation?
The authors undertake two parallel lines of work:

(1) Extending the study of Geeta et al with more data, consisting of both phylogenies and a shape classification dataset. The conclusion from this line of inquiry is that transitions from lobed to unlobed leaves are more common than transitions away from unlobed leaves.

(2) The authors conduct evolution simulations in a computational model of leaf development. Here, they look at {\it neutral} mutations and whether simply neutral evolution is sufficient to drive the observed trend.

The conclusion of the second part of the work is that the driver of the evolution toward simple leaf shape is entropy: there are more ways to make unlobed leaves than to make lobed leaves (at least in terms of gene regulation parameters that will produce the two leaf types). The argument is that random gene regulatory networks are more likely to produce unlobed leaves than lobed leaves; therefore, neutral evolution drives this trend.
Data Analysis:

Roughly $9000$ images of leaves were classified into 4 categories: unlobed, lobed, dissected, and compound. These labels were applied to the tips of 5 phylogenetic trees of angiosperms (3 resolved at the genus level and 2 at the species level). By fitting a continuous-time Markov chain to the labelled trees, the authors claim that there is a significantly higher rate of transition to the unlobed leaf shape compared to transitions to more complex shapes.
Simulation:

First, the authors validate a computational model (Runions et al) for leaf growth on an experimental dataset. By changing parameters in the model, they can recapitulate the morphological changes in the shapes of Arabidopsis leaves engendered by expression of two particular genes.

Then the authors run an evolutionary model (without selection, just random mutations) on top of the computational leaf development model. As the random walk in parameter space reaches a stationary distribution, they look at both the proportions of the leaf categories in the steady state as well as the transition rates between different categories. The result is that transitions to unlobed leaves are more common than from unlobed leaves.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for the helpful and clear summary of our work.

disp-quote.p: General Comments

The authors use angiosperm phylogenies from other works as the basis for the data analysis part of their work. Given the centrality of these phylogenies for their conclusions, more information is needed about how these phylogenies were constructed and what they mean. What is the timescale that they span? What method is used to infer them? What regions of DNA were sequenced in order to build the phylogenies? Also, maybe some more discussion of angiosperm evolution (e.g., when was the most recent common ancestor of all angiosperms?) would help put the study in context.

We also need a more in-depth discussion of the computational model. What are all the $>100$ parameters doing, and what informs the seemingly strange mutational model that changes parameters by 3 orders of magnitude?

I am confused about how the rates of transitions were inferred from the phylogeny. Here, one has a phylogeny inferred by some method (which needs to be described in more detail), and just the leaves are labelled. It is stated in the methods that BayesTraits was used to infer the transition rates. I realize this method is probably documented elsewhere, but a bit of a summary of how it works and how to interpret its results would (1) make the paper more selfcontained and (2) if the algorithm is credible, make the results firmer.

body.p: We thank the referee for the suggestion to make the paper more accessible. The tool we use to infer transition rates from the phylogenies, BayesTraits, is standard in the field. However, the referee is right that for an interdisciplinary journal, it may be helpful to more fully flesh out how these methods work. To that end, we have added an additional section S2.A "Phylogenetic rate inference" in the supplementary information that includes a longer description of how BayesTraits works, and how we used it to infer transition rates from phylogenies.

All trees are shown in the supplementary information section S2.B "Phylogenetic trees" with scale bars showing the amount of time or genetic change that the trees span. We have added details of the specific genes used to construct the trees in our analysis in Methods section F. For a broader discussion of angiosperm evolution, there is supplementary information section S4 "A short literature review of the adaptive significance of leaf shape".

Regarding the more in-depth discussion of the computational model, we have added supplementary information section S1.A "Leaf model details" to give a more detailed description of the leaf model. We chose our mutational scheme over other methods, such as uniform or Latin hypercube sampling, as the biologically relevant ranges for each parameter were unknown. Mutations of multiple orders of magnitude are a way to sample both parameters with large and small ranges with the same scheme.

Additionally, larger mutations help to move a walk out of a local region if it is stuck while small mutations ensure sensitive parameters are still varied. We use multiple schemes for additional robustness.

disp-quote.p: I am a bit skeptical of the authors' interpretation of the biological trend (of complex to simple leaf shapes) as being driven by neutral evolution. Why does one expect that the mutations generated by the random walk models described in the work are in fact neutral mutations?

body.p: A random walk is a well-established way of modelling the dynamics of neutral evolution in the monomorphic regime, where the population has a narrow diversity of different genotypes. In the higher mutation rate polymorphic regime, where the diversity of genotypes in the population is larger, we also expect that a random walk should still recapitulate the correct average transition rates. The purpose of the simulations is not to model every aspect of population genetics, but to ask whether developmental bias alone is sufficient to generate the observed directional asymmetry. By assigning equal fitness to all viable leaves, we isolate the contribution of development from that of selection. The agreement with the phylogenetic transition rates therefore demonstrates sufficiency rather than exclusivity: selection may also contribute, but it is not required to explain the observed bias. We discuss the evidence for the role of adaptation in leaf shape further in supplementary information section S4 "A short literature review of the adaptive significance of leaf shape".

disp-quote.p: - If the entropy of simple leaf shapes is higher than that of complex leaf shapes, why did we have complex leaves at all? I suspect the authors might argue that this is due to selection. In that case, what allows these complex shapes to become simpler? Wouldn't they be losing the selective advantage that drove them to be more complex in the first place? Or maybe the idea is that the rates are inferred assuming some steady state that generates the phylogeny? I did not understand this point.

body.p: The entropy language is a useful framing. Within that framework, one can view our study as showing that the entropy (defined here as the logarithm of the volume of parameter space mapping to a phenotype) of simple leaf shapes is higher than that of complex leaf shapes. If this entropy were to be ignored, and were we not to take fitness differences into account, then all states would be equally likely in our simulations. What we show is that the differences in entropy, which are related to differences in volumes of the parameter space that map to different phenotypes, also affect the rates. The inferred transition rates for both simulation and phylogeny from unlobed to more complex shapes are lower than the reverse but not zero. Therefore, complex leaf shapes arise stochastically through mutation and in this model would eventually reach a steady-state proportion, even in the absence of selection. This steady state proportion for complex leaves would be smaller than that of unlobed leaves, but non-zero.

disp-quote.p: Are the rates of transitions between leaf types inferred for the phylogeny assuming that the phylogeny is generated by the steady state of some Markov process? (I think the answer is no: in that case, how does one explain the initial condition?)

body.p: The tool we use to infer transition rates from phylogenies—BayesTraits—allows the initial state at the root of the tree to vary during the numerical optimisation (Pagel, 1994). Therefore, it is not assumed that the initial state is generated by the steady state of the Markov process.

disp-quote.p: If I take the mutation model (random walk) seriously, then shouldn't I expect that this steady state obeys detailed balance? In that case I should have piri→j=pjrj→i\begin{document}$p_i r_{i\to j} = p_j r_{j\to i}$\end{document} for each of the occupancies pi and transition rates ri→j\begin{document}$r_{i\to j}$\end{document} for the shape categories. How close are the rates inferred from the phylogenies to obeying detailed balance? Presumably, the Markov chain fitted to the simulation data obeys detailed balance because the mutation model itself does?

body.p: BayesTraits allows off-diagonal transition rates of the rate matrix to vary freely during numerical optimisation (Pagel, 1994). Therefore, there is no requirement for detailed balance to hold for the inferred rate matrix. For our simulations, the mutations are symmetric at the parameter level, therefore at this level, the process would be expected to obey detailed balance. We investigated this further by calculating the posterior signed equilibrium flux difference $\pi_iq_{ij}-\pi_jq_{ji}$ for all inferred rate matrices (see new material in supplementary information Fig S23). The posterior signed equilibrium fluxes for each transition pair in the simulations have 95% credible intervals overlapping with 0, which is consistent with detailed balance. Some phylogenetic state pairs are inconsistent with detailed balance. This could be due to something other than symmetric neutral drift acting on these specific transitions, such as selection or mutation biases not captured by the model. However, the identity of the transition pairs that are inconsistent with detailed balance varies between phylogenies, indicating that these apparent violations could be noise due to phylogenetic uncertainty. In any case, a violation of detailed balance does not disprove a developmental bias explanation, it just suggests that the underlying process is more complex than the reversible evolutionary algorithm we use in our leaf-model simulations. However, introducing non-reversible mutation dynamics into our leaf-model simulations would require additional assumptions and parameters describing mutational asymmetries, which are not necessary to reproduce the key bias towards unlobed.

disp-quote.p: I find it hard to take the discussion of development seriously without some consideration of mechanics. Presumably, the mechanics are hidden in the computational leaf development model, but this model is not discussed in enough detail for the reader to know. It seems to me that the interesting question is: what are the {\it mechanical} constraints on development that drive the apparent trend in evolution towards simpler leaf shapes? Maybe it is something about the type of differential growth needed to make complex leaf shapes less robust to mutation. But in this case, I would assume that selection plays a role in the complexity of shape. In any case, a better understanding (or explanation) of the computational model is needed to make this interpretation.

body.p: We thank the referee for the suggestion to make the paper more accessible. We have added a new, more detailed and pedagogical description of the model from (Runions, Tsiantis and Prusinkiewicz, 2017) in the supplementary information section S1.A “Leaf model details". We also note that Fig. 5 in the methods gives an overview of how the model works, including some mechanical aspects of development and growth.

More generally, mechanics is one component of the developmental map that determines which parameter combinations produce viable leaf morphologies. Our analysis concerns the geometry of this complete developmental map, irrespective of whether its constraints arise from gene regulation, tissue mechanics, or their interaction.

On the interesting question of what is causal, perhaps the example in figure 2 is helpful. We focus on two parameters, a morphogen repression strength, and a duration of growth. A key physical process here is called webbing, where cellular growth fills in the gaps between branching veins. This process flattens the leaf structure and creates a continuous, solid leaf blade (lamina). Strong webbing, characterized by a significant resistance to stretching and bending, results in a smoother margin (Runions, Tsiantis and Prusinkiewicz, 2017). The morphogen repression strength affects the physical parameters that determine how strong the webbing is. The duration of growth determines how long the leaf has to grow. If an unlobed leaf has some marginal patterning that results in small protrusions, such as serrations, increasing the duration of growth will amplify these protrusions, eventually forming lobes. Similarly, increasing the strength of morphogens that repress growth along the margin will deepen the sinuses between protrusions, resulting in lobes. Combinations can result in highly dissected and compound leaves, as illustrated in figure 2. Conversely, decreasing either or both will result in a smoother margin and eventually leaves with an unlobed shape. Thus, varying these two developmental parameters varies the physical processes that determine leaf shape. The mechanics of growth operate downstream of these parameters that we vary in our evolutionary simulations according to the details of the leaf developmental model.

disp-quote.p: Some discussion of timescales is needed, especially when invoking neutral evolutionary arguments. If a neutral mutation occurs, its time to fix in a population of size $N$ is $\sim N$ generations. What are the relevant angiosperm population sizes and the number of mutations that separate branches on the tree? Are timescales remotely consistent with e.g., the age of angiosperms on Earth?

body.p: Neutral processes have a well-established role in key aspects of angiosperm evolution, for example genome complexity (Lynch and Conery, 2003). This would suggest that the relevant timescales and generation times are not completely prohibitive of neutral processes also playing a role in the evolution of angiosperm leaf shape. Effective population sizes in plants are highly variable but estimates span 10^3-10^6. Assuming diploidy (and therefore average fixation time of 4Ne) and generation times of 1-10 years, this gives fixation timescales of 10^3-10^7 years. This is within the timescales of the trees we analyse, which span >150 million years.

disp-quote.p: Strengths:

The paper's underlying question is interesting, extending the authors' prior work on RNA along similar conceptual lines. The paper combines both image analysis of leaves and a computational analysis of a simple model of leaf development.
Weaknesses:

The entire paper is based on the Runion model. More intuition about the Runion model would be useful for a broader readership that cares about the evolutionary aspect of this, but may not know the developmental model in question. Obviously, this is prior well-established work, but 2 - 3 sentences highlighting the key structural aspects of such a model would be great.

Currently, that intuition is found implicitly in a sentence on page 2 ("complex leaf shapes need more specificity in their GRNs than their simpler unlobed leaf shape"), but the reader is left wondering - is the Runion model a detailed mechanistic one with multiple interacting genes/proteins? If so, how many? Or is it just 2 - 3 genes but with complexity entirely in how long they are each expressed/when they are turned off, etc.

body.p: We thank the referee for the suggestion to make the paper more useful for a broader readership. To that end, we have added a more detailed description of the (Runions, Tsiantis and Prusinkiewicz, 2017) model in supplementary information section S1.A "Leaf model details".

disp-quote.p: The Runions model has nearly 100 free parameters. Random walks in 100dimensional spaces have generic properties like a tendency to move toward regions of larger volume that have nothing to do with leaf biology. How do you disentangle the geometry of high-dimensional random walks from genuinely biological developmental bias? Would a toy model with 100 parameters and arbitrary phenotype categories also show "bias toward simplicity" if "simple" phenotypes occupy more volume?

body.p: Our argument is largely independent of the number of parameters. While it is true that most of the volume is near the surface in a high-dimensional space, our argument is about the relative volumes of the sets of parameters that map to each of the four phenotypes, an entropic argument if you wish. The basic intuition is that a simple phenotype needs fewer parameters to be fine-tuned, and so a larger volume of parameter space will map to a simpler phenotype.

The question about a toy model with arbitrary phenotypes is helpful because it allows us to clarify that what we are illustrating here with the biologically realistic example of leaf shapes is a much more generic principle. We can say with confidence that if the toy model generates a many-to-one set of outputs (phenotypes) through an algorithmic process whose description length does not grow faster than logarithmically with the size of the genotype space, then it should produce a bias towards simplicity regardless of the number of dimensions, see for example Johnston et al. (2022) and Dingle, Camargo and Louis (2018) for a longer discussion of this more general point which is based on arguments from algorithmic information theory (AIT). We do not use that framing in the current paper because the basic intuition for GRNs, that more complex phenotypes need more parameters to be fine-tuned and so have relatively smaller volumes, is more straightforward to understand than the more abstract AIT arguments. Our general prediction that this principle should hold more widely for GRNs can be made both by the more formal AIT route, or via the more heuristic fine-tuned parameter route.

It is also true that random walks can have biases towards regions of parameter space with high robustness (Van Nimwegen et al., 1999). For our model, this would mean a bias towards valid leaves, however we have no reason to expect this would bias the rates between different valid leaf shapes. We address this point in methods section C.

disp-quote.p: The discussion of Figure 4 (PCA of parameter space) uses "area" loosely when what's actually being measured is bin count in a 2D projection of a highdimensional space. I would think that, in general, PCA projections can be misleading about volume in the full parameter space, but I can't tell if that's an issue in this case. Some comments/thoughts here would be useful.

body.p: The quantitative estimate of phenotype frequencies is computed directly in the full parameter space and does not depend on PCA. We estimate that the total volume of viable leaves maps to simple unlobed leaves about 80% of the time. However, the volume is extremely high-dimensional, and so hard to visualise. PCA is used solely to provide an interpretable visualization of this otherwise high-dimensional structure. The PCA plots in Fig 4 and Fig S16 are there to be illustrative, not quantitative. Because the volume differences are large, we do not think that the projections of the main PCA components would be misleading on at least the ordering of the sizes of the parameter space components that map to each leaf shape. We provided a similar analysis for other projections -- PC1-PC6 (supplementary information section S3.B "PCA occupancy for higher dimensions"), finding the same trend. To make this point clearer, we have now changed the sentence in the Fig. 4 caption slightly “This (reveals that --> illustrates how) unlobed leaves occupy a larger region of model parameter space than more complex shapes and that this larger space also contains the majority of more complex leaves.”

disp-quote.p: The classifier validation section is in the Methods section, but it seems critical to the whole story. The < 80% agreement with manual classification could propagate to the rest of the estimates in the paper. Again, some comments/thoughts here would be useful.

body.p: The review raises a valid concern. In response, we have repeated the analysis of the agreement between by-eye and automatic morphometric classification and produced a confusion matrix for the two classification methods to make the uncertainty clearer (see supplementary information Fig S7, section S1.E). The confusion matrices show that the agreement between the by-eye and automatic morphometric methods is high for unlobed, dissected and compound. The main source of disagreement is leaves that were classified as lobed by eye being classified as either unlobed or dissected by the automatic morphometric method. The proportion of by-eye lobed leaves classified by the automatic-morphometric method as either unlobed (27%) or dissected (23%) is relatively balanced, which we think will cancel out some error as well. Moreover, we find that the agreement between the automatic-morphometric method and by-eye classification increases to 90.0% when using the categories unlobed and all other categories grouped into one (complex). This is the most important classification for our finding that development and phylogeny are both biased towards unlobed.

disp-quote.p: The authors should explain Mut2 and Mut5 in the main paper with a sentence or two, at least schematically, because how you mutate is obviously very relevant to interpreting a paper about biases in variation.

body.p: We agree that this information should be readily available in the main text. In response, we have added a sentence to the results section C for more detail on the random walk.

"[We mutated the initial sample using a random walk algorithm with two different mutational schemes, MUT2 (alg. 1) and MUT5 (alg. S2).] These algorithms work by iterating through model parameters one by one and perturbing the value by a small amount. We then [automatically classified the resulting shapes...]"
However, we note that in methods section C there is already a more detailed description of both algorithms.

“MUT2 (alg. 1) iterates through the parameters in a random order, and attempts to change the parameter by a value selected at random from an array of numbers randomly generated at 3 different orders of magnitude. MUT5 (alg. S2) is the same as MUT2 except that each mutation is additionally scaled by 10% of the current parameter’s range within the initial leaves (fig. S6). The aim here was to provide some way of accounting for the biologically relevant sampling range."
Moreover, the MUT2 algorithm is described in pseudocode in Algorithm 1 in the main text, and the pseudocode for MUT5 is in supplementary information section S1.C, as algorithm S2.

disp-quote.p: The two mutational schemes use additive perturbations to individual parameters. Real mutations presumably affect regulatory networks in more structured ways (e.g., changing binding affinities that affect multiple parameters simultaneously). How sensitive are the results to the assumption of independent single-parameter mutations?

body.p: The referee raises an interesting and well-known issue concerning this widely studied class of GRN models. Without a detailed understanding of how individual genetic mutations map onto model parameters, it is difficult to determine with confidence whether a mutation would produce correlated changes in certain sets of parameters. Our main argument, however, is that the primary source of the observed bias is geometric: the volume of parameter space (or equivalently, the entropy) corresponding to simple leaf morphologies is substantially larger than that corresponding to complex morphologies. As long as mutations explore parameter space approximately symmetrically, even if they involve correlated changes in multiple parameters, larger phenotype regions will tend to be encountered more frequently and retained for longer than smaller regions. We therefore expect the observed bias to be robust to many alternative mutation models, as is already supported by the agreement between our two mutational schemes, although quantifying this robustness is an interesting direction for future work.

disp-quote.p: The connectedness argument is made using a 2D PCA projection. Is there a way to check this statement in the full parameter space or perhaps in higherdimensional projections to test the robustness of this result? Connected components can merge/split under different projections.

body.p: We agree that the 2D projection alone is limited. We therefore performed a new analysis using the same method but in the full dimensional parameter space. The nearest neighbour graph for the full-dimensional data has the following numbers of connected components: unlobed-146, lobed-273, dissected-255, compound-315. This follows the same pattern identified for the PC1-PC2 projection, that unlobed splits into fewer connected components than other leaf shape categories. We have added this result to the caption in figure 9.
